Berlin: Language Science Press. DOI 10.5281/zenodo.14282808.
sources.note: Nothing: an identification study matching Oldendorp's numerals/lexicon to modern languages; for Okwa it records a one-word corpus and no identification ('Oldendorp's “Mangree” and “Okwa” could not be identified with any present-day language.. These cannot be ruled out to have been spurious', p. 40). No phonological remarks on any language.

sources.citation: Fogleman, Aaron Spencer & Robert Hanserd (eds.). 2022. Entry Nr. 048 'Un-named Okwa or Okoi Man'. In: 500 African Voices (online companion to Five Hundred African Voices: A Catalog of Published Accounts by Africans Enslaved in the Transatlantic Slave Trade, 1586-1936, Philadelphia: American Philosophical Society Press, 2022). Huskie Commons, Northern Illinois University. 6 pp. (2 cover pages + entry). CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
sources.note: Nothing. The whole document was read: catalog metadata (catalog no. 48, account recorded 1767-68, first published 2000-2002), source note (Oldendorp, Historie der caribischen Inseln.., kommentierte Ausgabe ed. G. Meier et al., VWB 2000-2002, vol. 1 p. 396), 'Comments: None', then the eight-sentence German passage and its English translation. It is ethnographic (scarification, deity names, gold and shell currency, rain-making sorcerers); the only Okwa lexical material is the four names Tschabee, Kinku, Ganetelli, Konfu, given without any remark on pronunciation, accent, stress or tone.

sources.citation: Sebro, Louise. 2010. Mellem afrikaner og kreol: etnisk identitet og social navigation i Dansk Vestindien 1730-1770. (Studia Historica Lundensia 15.) Lund: Lunds universitet. PhD thesis (history), 235 pp.
sources.note: no phonology content (history dissertation on ethnic self-identification in the Danish West Indies)

sources.citation: Oldendorp, Christian Georg Andreas. 1777. Geschichte der Mission der evangelischen Brueder auf den caraibischen Inseln S. Thomas, S. Croix und S. Jan. Theil 1. Barby. (BSB scan, archive.org item 11129612bsb, scanned text)
sources.note: Nothing. Okwa appears as an African 'nation' in ethnographic remarks (pp. 306-307) and with exactly one entry in the comparative vocabulary table of names for God: 'Okwa: Tschabee' (the scanned text). No other Okwa words, no grammatical or phonetic remarks.
